markers.title: One list, not two
markers.finding: The form asked for the incident type first, with options such as first aid or lost time that nobody can predict while their hand is under the cold tap, and hazard categories that contained events rather than conditions.
markers.decision: Incidents and hazards share one register. Type is a badge the manager can change on review, so nobody has to pick the right list before they can report.
markers.rejected: Separate Incidents and Hazards registers, which pushes the classification back onto whoever is reporting.

markers.title: The queue opens on what needs a person
markers.finding: Misclassified reports were sent back from above, and people learned that reporting was a way to get something wrong. The manager decided what was worth logging.
markers.decision: The first quick filter is Needs review, and each filter carries its own count, so the manager sees the work waiting on them before anything else.
markers.rejected: A severity-ranked default sort, which puts the classification decision back at the top of the page.

markers.title: The row names the person
markers.finding: People reported to a person, not a platform. Team members described telling the manager first, almost without exception.
markers.decision: Every row carries the reference, the reporter and the area under the title, so the list reads as things that happened to people on a shift.
markers.rejected: A reference-first row, which reads as a ticket queue and loses who it came from.

markers.title: Unclassified is a normal state
markers.finding: Incident type came first on the old form, and the notifiable-to-the-regulator question sent people to a compliance matrix that even area safety leads asked for help with.
markers.decision: The outcome column says Not yet classified until the manager sets it after the welfare check. An unclassified report is a stage, not an error.
markers.rejected: Defaulting new reports to the lowest severity, which makes them disappear from the work that needs attention.

markers.title: Status is the next action
markers.finding: Reporters rarely heard what happened next, and minor reports were closed without a word.
markers.decision: Status names what happens next and who owes it: welfare check due, action assigned, fixed awaiting sign-off. The list is a set of obligations, not a set of states.
markers.rejected: Open and Closed only, which hides the step the report is actually waiting on.

markers.title: The fix travels with the report
markers.finding: Minor reports were closed silently, and the reporting data could not show whether anything changed as a result of a report.
markers.decision: The last column carries the corrective action and its due date, and marks it overdue in the list, so a report and its fix cannot drift apart.
markers.rejected: An updated-at timestamp, which tells the manager that something happened but not what is owed.

markers.title: Telling the reporter is visible work
markers.finding: Reporters rarely heard what changed. The exception proved the point: the restaurant where a faulty piece of equipment was fixed the same day had a story people kept telling.
markers.decision: Closed reports stay on the page with a Reporter told mark against each one, so closing the loop is work that can be seen and counted.
markers.rejected: Archiving closed reports out of sight, which is what made the loop invisible in the first place.

markers.title: The manager lands on their own work
markers.finding: Managers were the gatekeepers of reporting and worked the system on behalf of their team, so the register is read by someone with a restaurant to run.
markers.decision: Named saved views with counts, defaulting to My open reports, so the page opens on this manager's queue rather than on everything ever reported.
markers.rejected: A single list sorted by date, which makes every manager build the same filter by hand every shift.
